title: Sparkling Water 12-pack

drivers.name: Price increase (3.5%)
drivers.evidence: Same price in Easter week (2026-03-30): sold 104 units (x1.29 vs baseline). No prior week at this price. Price increase typically reduces demand; 3.5% is non-trivial. No promotion this week.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 79.7. A 3.5% price increase to $6.17 is a known demand-lowering driver. Past promotions show average noise-adjusted lift of x1.84, but this week has no promotion—only a price hike. The week after a promotion (post-promo) typically sees x0.92, but no prior promotion occurred. The price increase is recent (same as Easter week 2026-03-30, which sold 104 units, x1.29 vs baseline). No prior week with this exact price existed. The historical trend shows growth (11% over 13 weeks), but baseline already reflects this. No event or promotion this week. The classical model’s 1.00 is too optimistic given the price effect. Use conservative shrinkage toward 1.0 due to limited data.

  shelf price: 6.17 (+3.5% vs regular price 5.96)

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 79.7 | 5%-95%: 42.9 - 198.7 | 10%-90%: 45.0 - 124.2

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-28% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
